The Beginning of the story
⍞ Materials: Sacajawea

➜ INTRO
By the age of 16, Sacajawea had been kidnapped from her tribe, gambled away to be a man's second wife, and was pregnant with that man's baby. That's when she would join the journey of Meriwether Lewis and William Clark down the Mississippi River and to the Pacific Ocean. But, where did her story begin?

Joseph Bruchac, will explore the early life of Sacajawea as well as recounting her journey with Lewis and Clark which became one of the most famous expeditions to take place in American History. While it is well researched and Joseph Bruchac uses primary sources, like the journals of Lewis and Clark, as support for the story, it remains a work of fiction. There is much that we don't know about Sacajawea's story.

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
Begin with the "Author's Note", p.195-199. Read the Prologue, Ch. 1.
• How different Sacajawea's life would have been if she had stayed amongst her people?

This historical novel is based on around the building of the transcontinental railroad which took place from 1863-1869. It was an arduous, dangerous job for the men who signed up to do it. Foot binding — the practice of applying tight binding to the feet of young girls to prevent further growth — was a Chinese custom historically associated with the wealthy. Small feet were considered more attractive and therefore necessary to find a more suitable partner. It was banned in 1911, but the practice continued in rural areas until circa 1949, when women were forced to remove the bindings on their “lotus feet” by governmental decree.

Meeting Louis Hughes
⍞ Materials: A Year in the South: 1865

➜ INTRO
In 1832, a baby boy is born around Charlottesville, Virginia. His name would be Louis Hughes and he was the son of a black mother and a white father. Louis would marry, have children and live through the events of the Civil War. In his old age, he would write a memoir, sharing his life story.
In A Year in the South, author and Civil War historian Stephen Ash, uses Louis Hughes' memoir and other additional primary sources to detail one of the most eventful years in the history of the United States: 1865. This is the year that the civil war would come to an end. But what did the victory of the Civil War mean for the men and women still enslaved in the South? When did freedom come? These are just a few of the questions, Stephen Ash will answer in his book.

Louis Hughes in the Spring
⍞ Materials: A Year in the South: 1865

➜ INTRO
Like many enslaved women and men, Louis Hughes had dreams of being free. He would run away a couple of times and every time he received a punishment. His story highlights the evil that we must face as those who study history. Humans are capable of great evil towards each other. Sin is a part of the human experience and we can trace it to every place and every time.

In his book, Why Study History, John Fea writes, "Indeed, anyone who studies the past realizes that there are no heroes in history. While people may perform heroic acts, all humans are tainted by sin and are susceptible to acting in ways that preference themselves over others and God. Historians understand, perhaps better than most, the reality of the pain, suffering, injustice, anger, and vice brought on by sin. In other words, they understand the tragic dimensions of life."

History reminds us of the inherent weakness in the human condition and the very real possibility that our fellow human beings are capable of horrendous things. This should humble us, for “there, but for the grace of God, go I.” One day there will be a new heaven and new earth where there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain.

➜ INTRO
1865 was a year faced with many uncertainties. As men and women were freed from the bondages of slavery, they would need to find homes, jobs and safe havens where they could relish their freedom. And households that had built their wealth on the backs of slaves, would need to transition quickly to be able to sustain themselves. The year 1865 would be one of the most tumultuous years in the history of the United States, but the fight for freedom didn't end with the emancipation proclamation or the winning of the civil war.
